strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and important problem: enabling accurate inference-time reward alignment of (distilled) flow/diffusion models by making value function estimation efficient. The framing that 'stochasticity is needed for value function estimation' is a clear and useful insight.

The two proposed designs are complementary and practically relevant: Posterior Diamond Maps (distilling GLASS Flows into one-step posterior samplers) offer O(N) consistency, while Weighted Diamond Maps (Prop. 5.1) work plug-and-play on off-the-shelf distilled flow maps, which makes the method immediately applicable to existing models like SANA-Sprint.

The theoretical development is solid and mostly self-contained: the derivation of the guidance formula (A.2), the Diamond DDPM sampling result (Prop. 4.3, showing the DDPM transition kernel is embedded in the Posterior Diamond Map via the early-stop reparameterization), and the weighted importance-sampling estimator with score-based correction (Prop. 5.1, proof in A.9) are carefully worked out, including closed-form g^{-1} for common schedules.
The Diamond Early Stop DDPM sampling is a neat practical contribution that reduces error accumulation of iterative denoise/renoise schemes, with supporting empirical evidence (Figure 4).

The large-scale T2I experiments are convincing for the Weighted variant: on GenEval with SANA-Sprint 0.6B at 1024x1024, the method outperforms Best-of-N, ReNO, and Prompt Optimization while being faster, and the Pareto-frontier analysis (Figure 6) demonstrates genuinely better scaling. Using GenEval as a disentangled metric mitigates reward-hacking concerns.

Honest acknowledgment of compute limitations for the Posterior Diamond Map experiments (small-scale CIFAR10/CelebA-64), and a useful ablation study on SNR, particle counts, and guidance time ranges (Tables 4-5).
weaknesses: The headline novelty claim ('first stochastic flow map') is somewhat overstated: the Posterior Diamond Map is a distillation of GLASS Flows (Holderrieth et al., 2025), and the Weighted Diamond Map renoising scheme closely resembles renoise-then-denoise importance sampling used in prior work (e.g., Wu et al. 2023 TDS, Feynman-Kac correctors, Sabour et al. 2025). The genuinely new elements are the early-stop reparameterization and the score-based correction terms; the relationship to these prior methods deserves sharper differentiation.

The 'consistency' guarantees (Prop. 4.1) are essentially straightforward Monte Carlo estimates under the assumption of a perfectly trained flow map; the effect of distillation error on the estimators is not analyzed empirically or theoretically, even though the paper's own Table 3 shows Diamond Maps have worse FID than standard flow maps. A variance/error analysis, especially for the log-sum-exp estimator whose finite-sample bias can be severe when the posterior is multimodal, is missing.

Baseline coverage for the large-scale experiments is narrow: no comparison with SMC/search-based methods (TDS, Feynman-Kac correctors, FPS, dynamic search) that are directly positioned as related approaches, and no error bars or significance testing on the GenEval results. The gains over ReNO (0.83 vs 0.81 mean, with Attribution actually lower: 0.65 vs 0.67) may be within noise.

There is an asymmetry between claims and evidence: the amortized/one-step posterior sampler (the core novel distillation) is only validated at small scale, while the strong large-scale results use the Weighted variant that requires a standard flow map, a differentiable reward, and guidance confined to a short time interval [0.05, 0.25], with notable sensitivity to hyperparameters (Table 5 shows performance varies by >1 point across configurations).

Several presentation issues reduce polish: inconsistent theorem/prop numbering ('Theorem 4.3'/'Theorem 5.1' in text vs Proposition in statements), a probable typo in Algorithm 2 line 14 (U_m <- U_m + V_m - V_m appears vacuous; presumably V_{t'} - V_t), typos ('that it not fully determined', 'that has has a goatee'), and equation (5) mixing variable names.
No code release is mentioned, and reproducibility of the high-resolution T2I results depends on unstated details (e.g., the composite reward weights).

The claim of exactness ('our method is not approximate but exact') applies only to the idealized setting; in practice all results depend on imperfect distillation, and the paper should temper this language.

strengths: The core idea—using stochastic flow maps to obtain consistent, one-step estimators of the value function and its gradient for reward alignment—is well-motivated and addresses a genuine bottleneck (biased denoiser approximation in guidance).

The theoretical development is largely coherent: the derivation of the tilted vector field (Eq. 11), the consistency of the MC value/gradient estimators (Prop. 4.1), the Diamond DDPM sampling result (Prop. 4.3, with a complete proof in A.8), and the corrected weighted estimator (Prop. 5.1, proof in A.9) are all worked out in detail.

Two complementary designs (Posterior vs. Weighted Diamond Maps) are presented with an honest discussion of the training-compute vs. inference-compute trade-off, including the O(N) vs. O(N/ESS) sample-efficiency distinction.

The large-scale T2I experiment (SANA-Sprint 0.6B, 1024×1024, GenEval evaluation) is a meaningful effort to validate beyond toy settings, and the Pareto-frontier analysis against Best-of-N (Fig. 6) supports the efficiency claim.
The ablations (SNR, particle count, guidance range; Tables 4–5) and the posterior-sampling error-accumulation analysis (Fig. 4, Diamond Early Stop DDPM) show care in experimental methodology.
weaknesses: Overclaiming of exactness: the paper repeatedly claims the estimators are 'not approximate but exact' and enable 'exact guidance,' but consistency holds only for a perfectly distilled flow map; in practice flow map error propagates through the recursive sampling/guidance procedure, and no error analysis or bound on this practical gap is provided.

Novelty positioning relative to closest prior work is thin: Sabour et al. (2025) already use flow-map one-step look-aheads with importance-sampling correction for reward alignment, and GLASS Flows (Holderrieth et al., 2025) already provide the stochastic transitions being distilled; the claim to be 'the first to construct a stochastic flow map' is not convincingly defended against these and the stochastic-interpolant literature.

The headline method (Posterior Diamond Maps) is only validated at small scale (CIFAR-10, CelebA), and the authors themselves concede compute limitations; thus the central claim of efficient accurate value-function estimation at scale rests on the Weighted variant, whose variance is never analyzed quantitatively (ESS is discussed only qualitatively).

Experimental rigor gaps: Table 1 reports single numbers without seeds, error bars, or variance; improvements over ReNO are modest (0.83 vs 0.81) and the method is actually worse on Attribution (0.65 vs 0.67); comparison baselines omit several relevant guidance/SMC methods (e.g., Feynman-Kac correctors, TFG) despite discussing them.

The estimators require a differentiable reward with backpropagation through the reward model (Algorithm 1, line 7), which excludes black-box rewards; this significant applicability limitation is not acknowledged.

No limitations section in the main text, no reproducibility statement or code release mentioned; several presentations issues remain (Proposition 4.1 mixes N and K, 'Theorem 4.3' vs 'Proposition 4.3' inconsistency, Fig. 1 caption garbled, undefined q_{1|t} in Section 5), suggesting insufficient polish.

The impact statement is boilerplate; given this is a method for steering generative models to arbitrary reward functions (with reward hacking observed and discussed via GenEval), a discussion of misuse considerations would have been appropriate.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated framing: the paper identifies value function estimation as the key bottleneck for exact inference-time reward alignment and proposes addressing it by re-designing the generative model rather than post-hoc approximations.

Two complementary methods: Posterior Diamond Maps (distilled stochastic flow maps with O(N) sample efficiency) and Weighted Diamond Maps (a plug-in estimator usable with off-the-shelf distilled flow maps), giving practitioners a practical training-compute vs. inference-compute trade-off.

The theory is complete and largely self-contained: consistency of the Monte Carlo value function and gradient estimators is proven (Props 4.1, 5.1), and Proposition 4.3 — that DDPM transitions are implicitly contained in the Posterior Diamond Map despite not being trained for it — is an elegant and non-obvious result, with a detailed derivation in A.8. The Diamond Early-Stop DDPM sampling is a clever way to reduce error accumulation in iterative sampling.

Weighted Diamond Maps are validated at meaningful scale: SANA-Sprint 0.6B at 1024x1024, evaluated on GenEval (a disentangled metric robust to reward hacking) rather than only the reward models used for optimization, and they beat Best-of-N, ReNO, and Prompt Optimization at lower wall-clock cost, with a convincing Pareto-frontier analysis across NFEs (Fig. 6).

Good reproducibility support: detailed architectures, hyperparameters, ablations over SNR, particle count, guidance steps, and time horizons (Tables 2, 4, 5), plus honest disclosure that the Posterior Diamond Map experiments are small-scale due to compute limits.
weaknesses: The consistency guarantees (Props 4.1 and 5.1) implicitly assume a perfect (or error-free) flow map. In practice, distilled flow maps have approximation error, which propagates through the value function estimates and renoising procedures; the paper provides no theoretical or empirical analysis of how this error accumulates or bounds the resulting bias in guidance/SMC, even though the abstract markets these as 'exact' methods.

The flagship Posterior Diamond Map is only evaluated on CIFAR-10 and CelebA-64 at 32-64px resolution, while its headline properties (exact posterior sampling, one-step DDPM transitions for SMC/search) are not demonstrated at scale. The at-scale validation covers only the Weighted variant, so the claimed superiority of the Posterior design (O(N) vs. O(N/ESS)) is empirically untested in realistic settings.

In Table 3, the Diamond Map's FID is noticeably worse than the standard Flow Map at higher step counts (e.g., 6.732 vs. 4.880 on CIFAR-10 at 8 steps), which the paper downplays as 'almost on par'; a more careful discussion of this quality trade-off is warranted.

Baseline coverage in the high-resolution experiments is somewhat narrow: comparisons are against Best-of-N, ReNO, and Prompt Optimization, but not against SMC/search-based inference-time alignment methods (e.g., Feynman-Kac correctors, dynamic search) that are cited as the closest competitors, and Table 1 lacks variance/confidence intervals.

The Weighted Diamond Map estimator requires differentiable rewards, backpropagation through the flow map, a trapezoidal quadrature approximation of the gamma-coefficients, and a tuned SNR ratio lambda; the sensitivity to these approximations and hyperparameters, and applicability to non-differentiable or black-box rewards, is not analyzed.

Originality is incremental in parts: the method is largely a careful combination of existing components (GLASS Flows, flow map distillation losses, importance/recovery-weighted sampling, DDPM reversals), though the synthesis and the Prop. 4.3 observation are genuinely new.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated central idea: amortizing posterior sampling (via GLASS Flows distillation) or stochastic renoising of flow maps into one-step 'look-aheads' makes consistent value function estimation tractable, enabling exact guidance, SMC, and search at inference time. This reframes reward alignment as a property of the generative model itself rather than a post-hoc sampler modification.

Two complementary designs with different practical trade-offs are well justified: Posterior Diamond Maps (higher ESS, needs distillation of GLASS Flows) vs. Weighted Diamond Maps (works off-the-shelf with standard flow maps). The paper discusses the ESS/importance-sampling view of both methods thoughtfully.

Theoretical contributions are substantial and mostly proven in detail: consistency of the MC value function and gradient estimators (Prop. 4.1), the elegant Diamond Early-Stop DDPM result (Prop. 4.3, showing DDPM transitions are contained in the Posterior Diamond Map with a full joint-distribution proof), and the corrected Weighted Diamond guidance estimator (Thm 5.1) with recovery-reward and score corrections, including a general stochastic operator extension.

Broad and convincing empirical evaluation: posterior sampling quality (Tables 3-4), inverse problems with Pareto/NFE analysis (Fig. 5, 11, Table 6), prompt alignment with held-out rewards to check reward hacking (Fig. 16), SMC scaling ablations (Fig. 14), and high-resolution T2I on FLUX and SANA-Sprint evaluated on disentangled benchmarks (GenEval, UniGenBench++). The NFE-based compute scaling comparisons against Best-of-N and Flow Map Guidance (Fig. 8-9, Table 1) are a particularly convincing demonstration that MC-sample scaling is a distinct and steeper scaling axis.
Honest and substantive limitations discussion (variance blow-up when prior support misses high-reward regions; inherited error from imperfect distillation).
weaknesses: There is a notable gap between the theory and the implementation. The paper's central selling point is 'exact/consistent' guidance, yet in practice the full analytical weights of Thm 5.1 are abandoned: importance weights are reduced to softmax(r) only, and gradient terms are individually unit-normalized and combined with a hand-tuned λ (Sections 'Implementation Details', D.2.1). This makes the deployed estimator a well-engineered heuristic rather than the theoretically grounded one, and the framing of 'exact guidance' in the introduction overstates what the experiments validate.

Posterior Diamond Map sampling quality lags the underlying flow map (Table 3: e.g., ImageNet FID 10.74 vs 6.06 at 1 step), so part of the framework's benefit rests on a distilled model that is still measurably inferior to its teacher; the posterior recovery advantage is mostly demonstrated against GLASS Flows, a very slow baseline in that comparison.

The ablation findings are somewhat favorable-mixed: particle scaling saturates quickly on SANA-Sprint (Table 7) and guidance-steps scaling shows diminishing returns, which softens the 'scales better than existing methods' narrative in some regimes; the strongest scaling story is specific to the FLUX setting.

Reproducibility concern: the code link in Section D is blank ('Code for our experiments can be found under .'), which undermines reproducibility for a methods paper with many hyperparameters (SNR schedule, guidance windows, normalization, MC schedules).

Presentation issues reduce polish: multiple typos and grammatical errors ('th problem', 'classwhile', 'compute-optimla', 'variery'), inconsistent numbering conventions (Prop. 4.1 referred to as 'Theorem 4.1' in A.3; Thm 5.1 statement uses mismatched index ranges), and a statement of Thm 5.1 whose notational density makes the method harder to follow than necessary.

Evaluation is restricted to image domains (and small/medium prompt sets, e.g., 30-50 prompts for ImageNet alignment), while the framework's generality claims span molecules, robotics, video, and audio; no empirical support is given for these claims.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: the paper identifies that consistent value function estimation—which underlies exact guidance, SMC, and search—is intractable with standard (deterministic) flow maps, and that stochasticity is the missing ingredient. This is a genuinely useful reframing of the reward-alignment problem around model design rather than post-hoc fixes.

Posterior Diamond Maps are a clean and interesting construction. Proposition 4.3 (showing that DDPM transition kernels are recoverable in one step from a posterior flow map via 'early stopping' on the inner time axis) is an elegant result, and the empirical demonstration that early-stop DDPM sampling beats iterative denoise-renoise (Figure 4, Table 5) is convincing and practically relevant for SMC/search proposals.

The evaluation is unusually broad for this line of work: controlled experiments on CIFAR-10/CelebA-64/ImageNet with FID/LPIPS/KID metrics, NFE-matched Pareto comparisons against DPS, flow-map approximation, Best-of-N, and Flow Map Guidance, plus high-resolution text-to-image experiments on SANA-Sprint 0.6B and a FLUX flow-map distillation evaluated on reward-disentangled benchmarks (GenEval, UniGenBench++). The scaling analysis (Figures 8-9, 14) directly probes the paper's central claim that Monte Carlo particles are a useful compute axis.

The limitations section is honest and substantive: it correctly identifies the variance blow-up when the prior poorly covers high-reward regions, and that distillation error is inherited by the estimators rather than caused by them.

The related-work positioning is careful, particularly the distinction from Sabour et al. (2025a) and LATINO (value function estimation rather than one-step lookaheads), and from approximate posterior learners (Gaussian mixtures, scoring-rule methods).
weaknesses: There is a significant gap between the theoretical claims and the deployed method. The paper's headline claim is 'exact'/'consistent' guidance, and Theorem 5.1 derives precise importance weights (recovery likelihood, score correction, gamma terms). Yet in Section D.2.1 the authors state they 'drop the analytical weights entirely,' use only softmax(r) weights, unit-normalize each gradient term, and add a shared hyperparameter lambda. The estimator actually used in the strongest experiments is therefore a heuristic variant of the proven-consistent estimator, which weakens the central soundness claim that distinguishes this work from existing biased guidance methods. This deviation deserves to be in the main paper with an analysis of when consistency is lost, not only in the appendix.

Consistency of all estimators holds only for a perfectly trained flow map/posterior sampler, and no theory or experiments quantify how distillation error propagates into value-function bias. Given that Table 3 shows the Posterior Diamond Map's unconditional FID is notably worse than the plain flow map (e.g., ImageNet: 10.74 vs 6.06), the practical accuracy of the 'exact' estimators on downstream tasks rests on a sampler with measurable degradation, which is under-analyzed.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: the code statement in Section D reads 'Code for our experiments can be found under .' with an empty URL. For a paper whose value depends on nontrivial implementations (GLASS distillation, Tweedie-based score recovery for SANA-Sprint, NFE accounting conventions), the missing code link is a concrete deficiency.

Novelty is partly incremental relative to GLASS Flows (Holderrieth et al., 2025): the Posterior Diamond Map is essentially a flow-map distillation of a GLASS velocity field, with the main new technical content being the early-stop/DDPM result and the weighted-renoising correction. The Weighted Diamond Map correction terms are close in spirit to importance-sampling corrections already used with flow-map lookaheads (Sabour et al., 2025a). The paper is a useful synthesis, but reviewers should not over-credit originality.

Several experimental comparisons have confounds: SANA-Sprint baseline results in Table 1 are imported from Eyring et al. (2025) rather than re-run under identical conditions; 'best result over ablated parameters' is reported for metric results (Section D.1.3), which introduces selection bias against baselines; and compute cost of K Monte Carlo samples per guidance step is nontrivial, with the paper's own SANA-Sprint ablation (Table 7) showing diminishing returns beyond K=4.

The manuscript has noticeable polish issues that occasionally impede clarity: e.g., 'The proof is simple and follows and the reparameterization trick' (Section 4), 'compute-optimla', 'model classwhile', an incomplete sentence in Section 4.1, and inconsistent labeling of results as 'Proposition' vs 'Theorem' between main text and appendix.

strengths: The central idea is well-motivated and timely: value function estimation is the key bottleneck for exact inference-time reward alignment, and the observation that stochasticity (rather than deterministic flow maps) is required for consistent exploration is crisp and clearly argued.

The two proposed designs are complementary and practically useful: Posterior Diamond Maps (distilling GLASS Flows into a one-step posterior sampler) and Weighted Diamond Maps (turning off-the-shelf flow maps into consistent value-function estimators via renoising plus importance weights). The Weighted variant in particular is attractive because it needs no retraining of the base model.

The theoretical results are largely sound and non-trivial: the consistency proofs (Propositions 4.1 and 5.1), the derivation of the tilted velocity field (10), and especially Proposition 4.3 showing that the Posterior Diamond Map contains an exact one-step sampler of the DDPM time-reversal kernel are nice contributions with complete derivations in the appendix.

Experiments are unusually broad for this line of work: posterior sampling and inverse problems on CIFAR-10/CelebA/ImageNet, plus high-resolution text-to-image on two architecturally different flow maps (velocity-parameterized FLUX and direct-prediction SANA-Sprint). Evaluating on GenEval/UniGenBench++ that are disentangled from the reward models mitigates reward hacking concerns.

The compute scaling analysis (Figures 8-9) is informative: Diamond Maps show a steeper NFE-quality Pareto frontier than Best-of-N and Flow Map Guidance, with the MC-sample count as a novel scaling axis, and the total NFE accounting is spelled out explicitly.
The limitations section is honest and identifies real issues (high variance when prior support mismatches the reward-tilted distribution; inherited error from imperfect distilled teachers).
weaknesses: There is a significant gap between the theory and the method actually used in the headline experiments. The proven consistent estimator of Proposition 5.1 is not what is deployed for text-to-image generation: the implementation drops the analytical weights, uses reward-only softmax weights, unit-normalizes each gradient term independently (D.2.1), applies the Tweedie approximation (25), trapezoidal quadrature for gamma, and a best-of-rollouts selection rule. This is a reasonable engineering compromise, but it weakens the paper's central 'exact/consistent guidance' claim, since the celebrated consistency guarantees do not apply to the configuration producing the main results (Table 1, Figures 8-9).

Novelty is incremental relative to very recent prior work. The GLASS reparameterization (sufficient statistic, time reparameterization, GLASS velocity field) is taken nearly wholesale from Holderrieth et al. (2025), and the Weighted Diamond Map is closely related to the renoising + importance-correction ideas of Sabour et al. (2025a/b) and LATINO. The contribution is the combination (distillation of stochastic transitions into a flow map, plus correction terms), which is solid but builds heavily on these precedents.

Reproducibility is compromised: the code link is an empty placeholder ('Code for our experiments can be found under .'). Given the many non-obvious implementation details (guidance windows, SNR schedules, loss reweighting, initialization networks), the broken link is a material concern for a paper whose practical pipeline involves many unstated approximations.

Some experimental results undercut the claimed advantages: the Posterior Diamond Map has consistently worse FID than the plain flow map at pretraining (Table 3, e.g., 10.74 vs 6.06 on ImageNet), i.e., there is a real quality tax for the posterior model, and the quantitative gains on GenEval/UniGenBench++ are moderate (0.785 vs 0.737 FMG / 0.748 Best-of-N).

Missing baselines: for value-function-based SMC/search alignment, closely related particle methods such as Twist (Wu et al., 2023a), TDS, and Feynman-Kac correctors (Skreta et al., 2025) are discussed but not compared against empirically, which makes it hard to assess the claimed efficiency advantage for SMC.

The paper claims rigorous 'exactness' language ('our method is not approximate but exact', Section 6) that is overstated: all practical results rely on imperfect distilled teachers, finite Monte Carlo samples (often mc=4), and multiple numerical approximations. The asymptotic/ideal-model distinction should be maintained consistently throughout.

Presentation issues: inconsistent labeling of Propositions as Theorems (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 5.1 vs. Proposition 4.3/5.1), a sentence fragment in the Proposition 4.1 proof sketch ('follows and the reparameterization trick'), typos ('th problem', 'compute-optimla', 'classwhile'), duplicated references (Liu et al., Flow-GRPO listed twice), and a reference with no year (Abdolmaleki et al.). These do not obscure the science but indicate the manuscript needed another editing pass.

The comparison between the two designs is left largely as an 'open theoretical question' (Section 5 discussion) without even controlled empirical head-to-head results under matched budgets on the same task, which limits the paper's ability to give practitioners actionable guidance.
